Verb: mine. It already ends in -e. (mine)
Regular verbs that already end in “-e” (mine → mined) just add “-d”.
Verb: craft – a regular verb. (craft)
“Craft” is an ordinary regular verb: just add “-ed” → crafted.
Verb: try – it ends in consonant + y. (try)
Spelling rule: when a verb ends in consonant + y (try), the “y” becomes “ied” → tried.
Verb: stop – short vowel + one consonant. (stop)
Short verbs with a short vowel + one final consonant (stop) double the last consonant → stopped.
Verb: play – there is a vowel before the y. (play)
Careful! If there is a vowel before the “y” (a, e, o, u, as in “play”), the “y” stays → played (NOT plaied!).
Verb: drop – short vowel + one consonant. (drop)
“Drop” is short and ends in vowel + consonant (o + p) → the “p” doubles: dropped.
Verb: study – there is a consonant before the y. (study)
In “study” there is a consonant (d) before the “y” → the “y” becomes “ied”: studied.
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: -ed spelling with “carry”)
Clue: carry ends in consonant + y.
In “carry” the consonant “r” comes before the “y”, so the “y” becomes “i” + “-ed” → carried.
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: doubling with “plan”)
Clue: plan has a short vowel and ends in one consonant.
“Plan” has a short stressed vowel before a single consonant → the “n” doubles: planned (“planed” means smoothing wood with a plane).
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: “visit” & “stay”)
Clue: visit is stressed on the first syllable; stay has a vowel before the y.
“Visit” is stressed on the first syllable (no double t → visited), and “stay” has a vowel before the “y” (→ stayed).
Verb: build – irregular, no -ed. (build)
“Build” is irregular: build – built – built. Never “builded”!
Verb: dig – irregular. (dig)
The 2nd form of “dig” is “dug” (dig – dug – dug).
Verb: find – irregular. (find)
“Find” becomes “found” in the Past Simple (find – found – found). “Founded” means started something, e.g. a company.
Verb: go – irregular. (go)
One of the most important irregular verbs: go – went – gone. In the Past Simple it is always “went”!
Verb: fight – irregular, spelt with “ou”. (fight)
“Fight” has the irregular 2nd form “fought” (with “ou”, just like bought and thought).
Verb: break – irregular. (break)
break – broke – broken. For the Past Simple you need the 2nd form: “broke”.
Verb: buy – irregular, spelt with “ou”. (buy)
buy – bought – bought. Don't mix it up with “brought” (from bring)!
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: “fall” & “lose”)
Clue: you need the past of fall and the past of lose.
fall – fell – fallen and lose – lost – lost. “Felt” comes from “feel”, not from “fall”!
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: “see” & “swim”)
Clue: you need the past of see and the past of swim.
Both verbs are irregular: see → saw (2nd form) and swim → swam (2nd form).
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: “write” & “win”)
Clue: you need the past of write and the past of win.
write – wrote – written and win – won – won. Both are in the 2nd form!
Negative of go – did not. (not go)
Golden rule: after “didn’t” you ALWAYS use the base form (infinitive) → didn’t go (NEVER didn’t went!).
A question about yesterday with the verb find. (find)
Past Simple questions are made with “Did + subject + base form” → Did you find...?
A What-question with the verb build. (build)
With wh-questions (What / Where / Why) too: “did” already carries the past, so the verb stays in the base form → What did Steve build?
Short answer: No + he + the helping verb from the question.
When a question starts with “Did…?”, you give a short answer with “Yes, … did” or “No, … didn’t”.
A negative Why-question with the verb take. (not take)
Negative wh-question in the Past Simple: “Why didn’t + subject + base form” → Why didn’t Lukas take...?
Negative of destroy – did not. (not destroy)
To make ordinary verbs negative in the Past Simple you always need “didn’t” + base form → didn’t destroy.
Short answer: Yes + we + the helping verb from the question.
To “Did you and Mia…?” the correct short answer is simply “Yes, we did!” (without repeating the main verb).
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: negatives with “didn’t”)
Clue: a negative with forget.
After “didn’t” the verb goes back to the 1st form (base form): “didn’t forget” – never “didn’t forgot”!
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: questions with “Did”)
Clue: a Where-question with download.
Question formula: question word (Where) + did + subject (you) + base form (download) → no “-ed” on the verb!
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: “didn’t” with irregular verbs)
Clue: the first half is negative (see), the second half is positive (mine).
The first part has “didn’t + base form” (didn’t see); the second part is a normal positive Past Simple statement (mined).
Verb: be – the subject is “I”. (be)
With I / he / she / it, the Past Simple always uses “was”.
Verb: be – the subject is “my friends and I”. (be)
“My friends and I” = we (plural) → so “were” belongs here!
Verb: be – a question with “you”.
With “you” it is always “were” – and with was/were you NEVER use “did”!
There + be – three pandas, plural. (There be)
“Three baby pandas” is plural → “There were”. For singular you use “There was”.
Negative of be – the subject is “the maths test”. (not be)
“The maths test” = it → the negative of “was” is simply “wasn’t” (no “didn’t”!).
The past of can. (can → Past Simple)
The past of “can” is “could”. It needs no “did” and is the same for every person.
There + be – one trapdoor, singular.
“A hidden trapdoor” is singular → so “There was”.
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: questions with “were”)
Clue: a question with be and “you”.
“was” and “were” are strong verbs: they need NO “did”! You just swap the subject and “were” → Were you tired?
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: “wasn’t / weren’t”)
Clue: a negative with be and “the villagers”.
“The villagers” = they (plural) → “weren’t”. With “be” in the Past Simple you never use “didn’t”.
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: “couldn’t”)
Clue: a negative with can.
“Couldn’t” needs no “did” and is always followed by the base form of the verb (“couldn’t light”).
Clue: “yesterday” is a finished time. (build)
The #1 trap! With time words like “yesterday” (finished past) you must NEVER use the Present Perfect (“have built”) – always the Past Simple: “built”!
Clue: a time phrase for “three months before now”.
In English it is “three months ago” – and “ago” always comes AFTER the length of time (“three months ago”, not “ago three months”).
Clue: “last night” is a finished time. (find)
“Last night” is a clear Past Simple time word! So “found”, not “have found”.
Verb: be – the subject is “I”.
“When I was ten years old” describes a finished point in the past → always Past Simple (“was”).
Clue: “in 2024” is a finished time. (release)
With past years like “in 2024”, English always uses the Past Simple → “released” (no Present Perfect!).
Clue: the week before this one – no “the”.
In English it is “last week / last month / last year” (without “the”!).
A When-question with the verb start. (start)
Questions with “When…?” ask about a specific point in the past → ALWAYS Past Simple (“When did you start…?”), never Present Perfect!
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: the perfect trap with “yesterday”)
Clue: “yesterday” is a finished time.
As soon as “yesterday” is in the sentence, “have played” is forbidden! And English word order is subject – verb – object – time.
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: word order with “ago”)
Clue: where does “ago” go?
Time phrases with “ago” go at the end of the sentence (or right at the start), and “ago” comes AFTER the length of time: “two days ago” + Past Simple (“saw”).
Which Past Simple sentence is grammatically CORRECT? (Focus: word order with time phrases)
Clue: subject – verb – object – place – time.
English S-V-O rule: subject (We) + verb (built) + object (a new base) + place (in Survival mode) + time (last night). No inversion like “Last night built we”!
mine → mined · craft → crafted
Basic recipe
You use the Past Simple for actions that are completely finished in the past (e.g. yesterday, last week, in the holidays). For most English verbs you simply add “-ed”.
Subject + base form + -ed  (the same for ALL persons!)
Brilliantly simple: in the Past Simple there is NO “-s” for he/she/it! I played, he played, we played – the same form everywhere.
Typical time words: yesterday, last week, in 2024, two days ago. If a verb ends in “-e” (mine, live, love), you only add “-d” (mined, lived).
No “-s” for he/she/it in the Past Simple!
With a silent “-e” at the end, you only add “-d”.
I mined sixty blocks of iron yesterday.
She crafted a new shield before the raid.
Spelling rules (-ed)
try → tried · stop → stopped · play → played
Spelling
With some regular verbs the spelling changes slightly when you add “-ed”. These 3 rules come up in almost every English test!
consonant + y → -ied  |  vowel + y → -yed  |  short vowel + consonant → double consonant + -ed
1) try → tried, study → studied, carry → carried. 2) play → played, stay → stayed. 3) stop → stopped, drop → dropped, plan → planned.
Careful with two-syllable verbs like “visit” or “open”: because the FIRST syllable is stressed, the last letter is NOT doubled (visited, opened).
Consonant + y becomes -ied; short “drop” doubles the p!
There is a vowel (a) before the y → the y stays!
Max studied his English words and then played Minecraft.
The skeleton stopped right in front of our wall.
build → built · go → went · find → found
Anvil knowledge
Many of the most common English verbs (go, build, find, fight, see) don't follow the “-ed” rule. They have their own 2nd form, which you have to learn by heart.
Subject + 2nd verb form (Past Simple)  — e.g. go → went, dig → dug
Important: you use the 2nd form ONLY in positive statements! As soon as “did” or “didn’t” comes in, the verb jumps back to the 1st form.
Don't confuse the 2nd form (Past Simple: broke, saw, went) with the 3rd form (past participle: broken, seen, gone). You only need the 3rd form for the Present Perfect or the passive.
Never add “-ed” to irregular verbs!
“seen” is the 3rd form – the Past Simple always uses the 2nd form “saw”!
We dug down to level -58 and found eight diamonds.
Leo fought the Ender Dragon and won the game.
Negatives with didn't
didn't go · didn't mine · didn't find
Most important rule!
When you want to say that something did NOT happen in the past, all ordinary verbs (except be & could) need the helping verb “didn’t” (= did not).
Subject + didn't + base form (1st form of the verb)
Memory trick: “Did already has the past in its inventory!” So the main verb after it ALWAYS stays in the base form (no -ed and no 2nd form).
The same for regular AND irregular verbs: “didn’t play”, “didn’t go”, “didn’t build”. The only exceptions: was/were (→ wasn’t/weren’t) and could (→ couldn’t).
The most common test mistake of all: never the 2nd form after “didn’t”!
In English, “not” can never stand alone in front of the main verb.
I didn't lose my sword because I kept it in my ender chest.
We didn't finish the roof before sunset.
Yes/no questions (Did you...?)
Did you find...? · Did he build...?
Yes/no questions
To ask a yes/no question about the past (“Did you…?”), you simply put “Did” right at the start of the sentence.
Did + subject + base form (1st form) + ...?
Here too, “Did” steals the past ending from the verb! So “Did you mine?” (NOT “Did you mined?”).
Many learners ask “Have you played yesterday?” – but for a finished past, English says “Did you play yesterday?”!
After “Did” you always use the base form “find”!
In English you can't just move main verbs to the front – you need “Did”.
Did you bring enough torches for the cave?
Did Tom finish his maths homework before Discord?
Wh-questions (What / Where / Why did...?)
What did you craft? · Where did they go?
Wh-questions
If you want more detailed information (What? Where? When? Why? How?), you simply put the English question word right before “did”.
Question word (What/Where/When/Why/How) + did + subject + base form?
Careful with “Who” as a subject question (“Who built that?”): there is no “did” → “Who built this castle?” (2nd form!).
In English, questions with “When…?” are almost always in the Past Simple (“When did you start?”), because they ask about a fixed point in time.
Base form “go” after “did”!
Don't forget the helping verb “did”!
Where did you hide the diamond chest?
Why did the Creeper explode near our farm?
Short answers (Yes, I did)
Yes, I did. · No, we didn’t.
Polite & correct
In English a single “Yes.” or “No.” often sounds too short or even rude. So with yes/no questions you add the pronoun + helping verb.
Yes, + pronoun + did.  |  No, + pronoun + didn't.
For questions with “Was/Were…?” you answer with was/were, of course (“Yes, I was.” / “No, they weren’t.”), not with did!
In short answers you NEVER repeat the main verb (so NOT “Yes, I did played”).
Short, snappy and perfect: just “Yes, I did.”
The helping verb in the answer always matches the question!
“Did you beat the Ender Dragon?” — “Yes, we did!”
“Did Mia lose her horse?” — “No, she didn't.”
was & were (statements)
I / he / she / it was · you / we / they were
The verb “to be”
“was” and “were” are the past forms of “be”. You use them to describe states, feelings, places and qualities in the past.
I / he / she / it + was   |   you / we / they + were
Remember “you”: even when you are talking to just ONE friend, English ALWAYS says “you were” (never “you was”!).
“could” behaves just as strongly as was/were: it doesn't need “did” either.
With “you”, standard English always uses “were”.
“My friends” is plural (= they) → “were”!
I was exhausted after I had built that huge bridge.
Our classmates were excited about the redstone lift.
wasn't / weren't & questions
wasn't · weren't · Were you...?
No “did”!
To make “was” and “were” negative or to ask questions with them, you need NO “did”! They are strong enough to do it themselves.
Subject + wasn't / weren't   |   Was / Were + subject + ...?
For questions, “Was” or “Were” simply moves to the front, before the subject: “You were online.” → “Were you online?”
The same goes for “could”: negative “couldn’t” (not “didn’t could”) and question “Could you…?” (not “Did you could…?”).
Never mix “did” with “was/were”!
The negative of “be” is always “wasn’t” or “weren’t”.
Were you scared when the cave sound played?
The server wasn't online during maintenance.
There was / There were
There is/are in the past (singular & plural)
Describing
Perfect for describing your Minecraft world or an adventure: “There was a cave…” or “There were three zombies…”.
There was + singular (a/an/one)   |   There were + plural (two, many, some...)
Negative: “There wasn’t any lava.” / “There weren’t any Creepers.” Question: “Was there a chest?” / “Were there any villagers?”
Many languages use one form whether there is one Creeper or ten. In English you have to watch for singular (was) vs. plural (were)!
Five zombies = plural → “There were”!
“There was / There were” – never “It gave” or “It had”!
There was a blacksmith with diamond boots in the village.
There were twenty torches lighting up the tunnel.
Time words (yesterday, ago, last...)
The time-portal markers of the Past Simple
Time compass
In tests, time words tell you straight away that you need the Past Simple. They show that a point in time is completely in the past.
yesterday · last night/week/year · [time] + ago · in 2023 · when I was...
English word order: time phrases go at the END of the sentence (or right at the start) – never between the verb and the object!
“two days ago” (ago comes AFTER the number). “last week” (WITHOUT “the”!).
“ago” comes after the length of time, and the time phrase goes at the end of the sentence.
In English the subject always stays before the verb (we played)!
We defeated the Ender Dragon two weeks ago.
Last night I built an automatic bamboo farm.
The present perfect trap
Past Simple vs. Present Perfect
Creeper trap #1
Many languages tell stories with a “have + participle” form. If you carry that over into English (“I have played yesterday”), the sentence explodes like a Creeper!
Fixed point in the past (yesterday, last, ago, When...?) → ALWAYS Past Simple!
English uses the Present Perfect (“I have played”) only without a fixed time in the past (e.g. life experiences: “Have you ever played Minecraft?”).
Rule of thumb for school: if you see yesterday, last…, …ago, in 2022 or When…? → hands off have/has! Use the Past Simple!
“yesterday” + Present Perfect is always wrong in English!
“When…?” asks about an exact point in time → Past Simple!
I visited my grandma last Sunday.
We watched a cool Minecraft tutorial ten minutes ago.
